transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical. Like, I’ll be convinced I put a wrong number in a data release at work. I do a lot of statistical analysis, and honestly, the software my company uses is so incredibly outdated. I keep telling my manager that we need to migrate to a newer system because the interface is just gray and tiny, and I actually had to get reading glasses this year just to see the screen properly. Fifty-three creeps up on you, I guess, and the optometrist said my astigmatism is getting slightly worse, too. 

But anyway, it’s not just the data at work. It’s also things at home, like... thinking I left the back door unlocked, or that I paid a bill from the wrong bank account. Which reminds me, the city water company completely changed their billing portal last week and it’s a total mess to navigate. They didn't even send out an email warning us about the downtime. 

But the real issue I'm having is that even when I know I checked the door, or I know I checked the spreadsheet a dozen times, my mind just won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused some absolute disaster. I just can't shake the feeling.
Do you find yourself performing any specific rituals or repetitive behaviors in an attempt to calm down or make these unwanted thoughts go away?

Well, yes, to try and calm myself down I... I end up reopening the spreadsheets. Which, by the way, takes forever because the server lag is just atrocious right now. My coworker Dave—he sits two cubes down from me—he's always complaining about the network speed, but then he goes to lunch and leaves his computer completely unlocked. It’s a massive security risk! I’ve told him, 'Dave, you’re going to fail a compliance audit,' but he just shrugs it off. He eats these awful tuna sandwiches at his desk, too, and the smell just gets trapped in the office carpet. 

But, um, anyway, I reopen the files, and I'll reread my emails line by line. Which is where the new reading glasses come in. I actually got the frames at Costco. They have a surprisingly good optical department, much better than that place in the mall, and you can pick up bulk paper towels while you wait. 

But yes, I reread everything line by line, and at home, it’s the same thing with checking the locks and the payment confirmations. I check them over and over, and it has to be in a very specific set order. Like, front door, back door, garage. The garage door sensor is so finicky right now, a single leaf from my neighbor's oak tree will block it. I really need to ask him to trim those branches, but he's very defensive about his landscaping. 

But I have to keep doing my checks in that exact order until my brain finally feels like it's 'safe.' And the worst part is, because I'm doing all this... some nights I’m still sitting at my desk hours and hours later, and I have absolutely nothing actually finished.
Do you feel like these rituals and repetitive behaviors are interfering with your daily life or causing you a lot of distress?

Oh, absolutely. It's... it's taking over everything. Like I said, I sit there for hours, which means I’ve fallen way behind on my major work deadlines. I stay late reviewing things over and over, but I still don’t actually finish the reports. And when I stay late, I end up hitting the absolute worst of the evening traffic on the drive home. They’ve been doing construction on the highway for, what, three years now? It’s supposed to be a lane-widening project, but I swear I never actually see anyone working when I drive past. Just a sea of orange cones. They leave them out in all weather, and they get so grimy and faded. 

But because of all this checking, I really don't have a life outside of my house and the office anymore. I’ve completely stopped going to my Thursday salsa nights, and I haven't been kayaking all season. I just can’t get away from the checking and reviewing in time to actually make it out the door. Which really breaks my heart, because I bought these beautiful T-strap dancing shoes for the salsa club. They were shipped all the way from Spain, actually. The shipping took six weeks, and when they finally arrived, the cardboard box was completely crushed on one side! The post office is just so careless lately. Our regular mail carrier, Tom, retired back in April, and the new guy always leaves the mail half hanging out of the slot. Anyone walking by could just reach in and grab my bank statements, which is a whole other thing to worry about. 

But... yeah, I'm just so stuck in these loops that I can't do the things I enjoy anymore. It's causing me a massive amount of distress. I'm just exhausted all the time.
Do you feel like these unwanted thoughts are coming from your own mind or do they feel alien to you?

Oh, they're definitely from my own mind. I know it's me thinking them, even if I don't want to. It's just my brain getting stuck on overdrive, I guess. Sort of like how my car's engine has been acting up lately. I drive a 2014 Honda Civic, and it's usually so reliable, but the last few weeks it's been making this awful rattling noise whenever I idle at a stoplight. I took it into the mechanic—this guy named Sal over on 4th Street—and he tried to tell me it was the catalytic converter. But I looked it up online, and the symptoms just don't match. I really think it's the heat shield. Mechanics always try to upcharge you, especially if you're a woman. My sister had the exact same thing happen to her Toyota last year. She ended up paying almost eight hundred dollars for repairs she didn't even need. And she's a teacher, so it's not like she has that kind of money just lying around. She teaches second grade, and they don't even give her a budget for classroom supplies anymore. She has to buy all the construction paper and markers out of pocket. 

But anyway, what was I... oh, right. The thoughts. Yeah, they are definitely my own thoughts. They just won't shut up.
Do you experience excessive worry about everyday things, even when you're not having these unwanted thoughts about mistakes or unlocked doors?

Everyday things? Um... no, not really. If my brain isn't stuck on the locks or the work files, I'm actually fine. Like, I don't worry about normal day-to-day stuff. Take grocery shopping, for instance. I don't stress over it. Although, I will say they completely rearranged the aisles at the Safeway on Elm Street, and it makes absolutely zero logical sense. They put the baking supplies in the exact same aisle as the pet food. Who wants to look at wet cat food when they're trying to pick out vanilla extract? 

I have a cat, actually—a Maine Coon mix named Barnaby—and his prescription diet is just astronomically expensive lately. It went up by three dollars a can! I actually sat down and ran the numbers on it last weekend, and standard inflation doesn't even come close to accounting for that kind of markup. It’s pure corporate greed. I ended up sending a very detailed email to the manufacturer's corporate office with a statistical breakdown of their historical pricing trends versus the consumer price index. I haven't heard back, naturally. Customer service is just a joke now. You get stuck talking to those automated chatbots that just loop you back to the main menu over and over. It's infuriating. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, worrying about everyday things. No, I don't really have that. It's really just the checking loops that ruin my day.
Are you trying to prevent something bad from happening when you repeat these checks, or is it more about feeling less anxious?

Well, it's... I guess it's a bit of both, maybe? But mostly it's just about getting that awful, tight feeling in my chest to go away. To calm myself down, I end up reopening my spreadsheets, rereading emails line by line, checking the locks, checking the payment confirmations... and I have to do it over and over in a very specific, set order until it finally feels "safe." If I mess up the order, I have to start all over again. And some nights I'm still sitting at my desk hours later with absolutely nothing actually finished. 

It's actually a lot like how my desk at home is set up. I have this beautiful antique roll-top desk that I found at an estate sale out in Springfield. The woman who owned it before me must have been a seamstress or something because one of the little cubby holes still had a vintage wooden spool of thread in it. Real silk thread, too, not that cheap polyester blend they sell at Joann Fabrics nowadays. I went in there last week to buy some fabric for a set of curtains I was thinking about making, and the line for the cutting counter was just absurd. Only one person working, and of course, the customer at the front of the line had twelve different bolts of fabric, all needing fractional yardage cuts. And the scanner kept malfunctioning! I swear, they haven't upgraded their point-of-sale systems since 1998. The beep it makes is at this incredibly shrill frequency, it practically gives you a migraine just standing there. 

But, um... anyway. Yeah, I check things in that specific order just to make the anxiety stop so I can feel safe again, even though it means I never actually finish my work.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things like your health, finances, or relationships when you're not preoccupied with the specific thoughts about mistakes or unlocked doors?

No, not really. Like I said before, if I'm not stuck in one of my loops with the doors or the spreadsheets, I'm actually pretty calm about regular stuff. I don't sit around worrying about my health or my bank account or anything like that. I mean, I do keep a close eye on my finances, but that's just being responsible. I actually have this really intricate Excel workbook I built to track all my expenses. It's got pivot tables and automatic conditional formatting to highlight when a category goes over budget. I spent like, three whole weekends getting the macros to run perfectly. 

I actually learned how to write macros back when I took a few computer science classes at the community college. That was years ago, back when they still taught Visual Basic. The professor was this guy, Mr. Henderson, who always wore these terrible argyle sweater vests. Every single class, a different color argyle. He had this habit of jingling the change in his pocket while he lectured, and it drove me absolutely up the wall. It was just this constant *clink-clink-clink* the entire time he was talking about arrays and loops. I actually had to sit in the very back row just to muffle the sound a bit. And the chairs in that lecture hall were those awful plastic ones with the tiny little half-desks attached to the side, you know the ones? If you're left-handed, you're just completely out of luck. 

But, um... sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, worrying about other things. No, I don't really worry about my health or relationships or anything like that. It's just the checking.
Do you feel compelled to perform any specific physical acts, like touching or tapping, as part of your checking rituals?

Physical acts? Like tapping? Um... no, not tapping exactly. It's more about the actions themselves, like I mentioned before. I have to physically reopen the spreadsheets, reread the emails line by line, check the locks, check the payment confirmations... and it all has to be in that very specific, set order until it feels "safe." 

Speaking of the locks, I actually had to get a locksmith out to the house last month because the deadbolt on the back door started sticking. It was this older gentleman, probably in his seventies, and he drove this vintage Ford Econoline van. You don't see those much anymore. My uncle used to have one back in the late eighties, painted this awful mustard yellow color. We took it on a road trip to the Grand Canyon once, and the air conditioning went out somewhere in New Mexico. It was over a hundred degrees outside, and my cousin left a pack of crayons on the dashboard. They completely melted into this giant, rainbow-colored puddle right into the defrost vents. My uncle was so mad he didn't speak for the next two hundred miles. We ended up having to stay at this really rundown motel in Flagstaff where the pool was completely empty and filled with tumbleweeds. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the rituals. Yeah, so I just do those things—the spreadsheets, the emails, the locks—over and over. And like I said, some nights I'm just sitting at my desk hours later, and I haven't actually finished a single thing.
Are your checking rituals more about preventing something terrible from happening or about making the anxious feeling go away?

I think I might have mentioned this a little earlier, but it's really just to make the anxiety stop. To calm myself down, I end up reopening my spreadsheets, rereading the emails line by line, checking the locks and the payment confirmations over and over. 

Actually, speaking of payment confirmations, my firm just switched our whole accounting software to this new cloud-based platform last Tuesday. They brought in this outside consultant to train us, a young guy, maybe twenty-five, wearing these incredibly bright blue sneakers with a tailored suit. Who wears sneakers with a suit? Anyway, he kept using all these ridiculous corporate buzzwords like "synergy" and "bandwidth," and he brought in donuts for the whole team, but they were all vegan, gluten-free donuts from that new bakery over on Elm Street. Have you been there? I tried one that was supposed to be maple glazed, but the texture was exactly like a kitchen sponge. My neighbor Brenda absolutely loves that place, though. She goes every Sunday after her water aerobics class. She's been trying to get me to join her for water aerobics for months, but the chlorine just completely strips the color right out of my hair, and my stylist charges way too much for a touch-up for me to ruin it in a community pool. 

But, um... I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. Oh, right, the anxious feeling. Yes, so to calm down I have to do all those checks in a very set order until it finally feels "safe." And because of that, some nights I'm still sitting at my desk hours later with absolutely nothing actually finished.
Do you have any recurring, intrusive thoughts that aren't about making mistakes or unlocked doors?

Um, no, not really. It is pretty much just the mistakes with my work and the doors. I don't really get those kinds of thoughts about anything else. I mean, my brain is usually just so focused on the data. 

Speaking of which, I actually went out to buy a new monitor this past weekend so I could see my spreadsheets better at my home office. I went to that big electronics store out by the highway, and it was an absolute madhouse. They had this massive display of those new curved televisions right at the front. Have you seen those? I just don't understand the appeal, honestly. If you sit even a little bit to the side, the picture looks completely distorted. Anyway, the salesperson who helped me was this teenager who looked like he hadn't slept in a week. He kept trying to upsell me on this ridiculous gaming monitor with all these flashing LED lights on the back. I had to explain to him that I am looking at financial models, not playing whatever video games kids play now. 

My nephew plays that one game, Fortnite, for hours on end. He actually broke his headset last month because he threw it at the wall when he lost a match. My sister was furious. She made him pay for the replacement out of his allowance, which I think is completely fair. You really have to teach them the value of a dollar early on. When I was his age, I was making three dollars an hour babysitting for the neighbors, the Millers. They had this huge Old English Sheepdog that just drooled on absolutely everything...

But, um... gosh, I am sorry, I completely lost track of what you asked me. Oh, right, other thoughts. No, no, it is really just the work stuff and the locks. I don't have any other worries popping into my head like that.
Are there any parts of your life where you feel like these checking rituals are not causing problems or interfering with your daily activities?

Um, no, not really. It feels like it's interfering with absolutely everything lately. I've actually fallen way behind on my major work deadlines because, like I said, I stay late reviewing things over and over, but I still don't actually finish anything. And my personal life is just... well, non-existent right now. I've completely stopped going to my Thursday salsa nights, and I haven't been kayaking in months because I just can't get away from all the checking and reviewing in time to actually go anywhere. 

Speaking of kayaking, I used to go out on the reservoir every Saturday morning with my friend Diane. She has this beautiful, bright yellow fiberglass kayak that she bought at a silent auction fundraiser for the local animal shelter. They had all these amazing items—gift baskets, a weekend getaway to Napa, and even a signed jersey from some football player, though I don't follow sports so I couldn't tell you who it was. The shelter does such good work, though. They just took in a whole litter of stray kittens that were found under the bleachers at the high school. My neighbor Brenda actually adopted one of them, a little tuxedo cat she named Sylvester. She buys him these expensive organic cat treats that smell exactly like canned tuna. I was over there last week for coffee, and Sylvester just sat on the kitchen counter staring at me the entire time. It was a little unsettling, to be honest. Brenda said he's just "protective," but I think he was plotting something. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the checking. Yeah, it's definitely causing problems everywhere. I just can't seem to get away from it long enough to do the things I used to enjoy, or even just finish my work on time.
Do you feel like your checking rituals are mostly about preventing mistakes or is it more about needing things to be a certain way?

I think it's... well, it's really about preventing the mistakes, but also just needing that awful feeling to stop. Like I said before, to calm myself down, I just end up reopening all my spreadsheets, rereading every single email line by line, checking the locks, and going over the payment confirmations over and over again. And I have to do it in a very specific, set order until it finally feels "safe." 

Actually, speaking of emails, I got the strangest email yesterday from this company claiming I had won a cruise to the Bahamas. It looked so official, with the logos and everything, but the sender's address was just a bunch of random letters and numbers. My brother-in-law, Gary, actually fell for one of those scams a few years ago. He ended up giving them his credit card information because he thought he was getting a free set of golf clubs. He is obsessed with golf. He spends every Sunday out on the course, regardless of the weather. Once, he played through a torrential downpour and came home covered in mud, completely ruining the beige leather seats in his new sedan. My sister was absolutely livid. She made him pay for a professional detailing service, which I think cost him upwards of three hundred dollars. The guy who did the detailing, Marco, actually used to go to high school with me. He was always getting into trouble for skipping class to work on cars in the auto shop. 

But, um... gosh, I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. What were we talking about? Oh, right, needing things a certain way. Yes, so I have to do all those checks in that exact order until I feel safe, and because of that, like I mentioned, some nights I'm still sitting at my desk hours later, and I have absolutely nothing actually finished.
Do you feel like the things you check need to be in a specific order or arranged in a certain way for you to feel calm?

Yes, exactly, like I think I was just mentioning a second ago. It absolutely has to be in a very specific, set order. To calm myself down, I have to go through that exact sequence—reopening the spreadsheets, rereading the emails line by line, doing the locks, and then checking the payment confirmations over and over. 

If I don't do it in that exact arrangement, it just doesn't feel "safe," and I have to start the whole routine over. I've always been very particular about how things are arranged, honestly. Even my desk at the office has to be set up just right. I actually went to the office supply store last Tuesday to get these very specific fine-tip blue gel pens that I keep in a certain cup on my desk. I only write with those. Well, the cashier there—this older gentleman with a really impressive handlebar mustache—was telling me the manufacturer might discontinue them! Can you believe that? I panicked and bought four boxes just in case. 

My coworker, Greg, is always trying to borrow my pens, and it drives me crazy because he’s the kind of guy who chews on the caps. It is just incredibly unsanitary. He borrowed one of my yellow highlighters once and brought it back with the tip completely smashed and covered in black ink from dragging it over freshly printed documents. I ended up just throwing it straight in the trash. Greg also eats tuna salad at his desk every single day at 11:30 AM on the dot. The smell just lingers in the entire analytics department all afternoon. His wife makes it for him, and apparently, she puts sweet relish in it, which just seems wrong for tuna... 

But, oh, gosh, I am so sorry, I totally lost my train of thought again. What did you just ask me? Oh, right, the order of the checking. Yes. Like I was saying, it has to be that set order until it feels safe. And because I have to keep doing it over and over until it's perfectly in sequence, some nights I’m still sitting there at my desk hours later, and I have absolutely nothing actually finished.
Are there any areas of your life where you feel like you're still able to function normally and without significant distress despite these checking rituals?

No, honestly, I don't think there's any part of my life that's normal right now. I know I've mentioned this a couple of times, but it really is just taking over everything. I've fallen so far behind on my major work deadlines because I'm staying late every single night just reviewing the same things over and over, and I still don't finish anything. And my personal life... well, I've completely stopped going to my Thursday salsa nights, and I haven't been kayaking at all because I just can't pull myself away from the checking and reviewing in time to go anywhere. 

Actually, the last time I went to salsa class, I bought these gorgeous new dancing shoes. They have a two-inch heel and they're covered in this sparkly silver material. I found them at this little boutique downtown that sells vintage clothing and accessories. The owner, this woman named Beatrice, makes all her own jewelry out of recycled glass. She was telling me how she sources the glass from old soda bottles that she finds at antique fairs. She actually found a completely intact, unopened bottle of Coca-Cola from the 1950s once. Can you imagine? She said she sold it to a collector for almost five hundred dollars. I think collecting things is fascinating, though I don't have the space for it myself. My uncle Arthur used to collect stamps. He had binders and binders full of them, organized by country and year. When he passed away, my aunt didn't know what to do with them, so she just donated the whole collection to a local historical society. I hope they appreciated it, because he spent decades putting it together. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, functioning normally. No, it's just really bad everywhere right now. I can't get anything done at work, and I've basically given up all my hobbies because the checking just takes up all my time.
Do you feel like the things you check need to be symmetrical or exactly right for you to feel calm?

Yes, exactly right. I know I sound like a broken record today, I really do, but that's exactly it. Like I keep saying, to calm myself down, I have to reopen the spreadsheets, reread the emails line by line, check the locks, and go over the payment confirmations over and over again in that exact, set order. If it's not perfectly right, it doesn't feel safe. 

It’s a bit like when I’m building statistical models for my job, everything just has to balance out perfectly. Though, speaking of work, our new IT guy, Kevin, came in to update our department's server software yesterday. He is so incredibly loud when he types. He uses one of those mechanical keyboards that click-clacks loudly with every single keystroke, and it echoes through the entire analytics floor. He told me he actually built the keyboard himself from scratch. He ordered the individual keys from some specialty website in Germany. 

My nephew, Tyler, is really into building computers and electronics too. He’s nineteen and just started his sophomore year at Purdue. He’s studying agricultural engineering, which is so surprising because our whole family grew up right here in the city, so I have absolutely no idea where he got this sudden passion for farming equipment. Last Thanksgiving, he spent a solid hour explaining the mechanics of modern combine harvesters to my mother, who is eighty-two and mostly deaf in her left ear. She just nodded and smiled the whole time while eating her cranberry sauce. She makes her own cranberry sauce from scratch, actually, with fresh orange zest and just a tiny pinch of cinnamon. It’s a recipe she found in a magazine back in the late seventies, and she refuses to use the canned stuff... 

Oh, gosh, I am so sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? My mind just wanders off. What were you asking me? Oh, right, needing things to be exactly right. Yes, so like I said, I have to do my whole checking routine in that set order until it feels completely safe and right. And because I can't stop until it is, I end up sitting there at my desk for hours into the night, and I still have absolutely nothing actually finished.
Do you feel like the things you check need to have a certain level of precision or perfection to them, beyond just being correct?

Precision? Oh, absolutely. I mean, I feel like I'm just repeating myself at this point, I really do, but yes. It goes way beyond just being correct. To calm myself down, it’s not enough to just know the math is right. I have to reopen the spreadsheets, reread those emails line by line, check the locks, and go over the payment confirmations over and over again in that exact set order until it finally feels perfectly precise and "safe." 

Precision is just... well, it's everything in my line of work. Working with data and numbers all day, you get used to things being exact. Actually, I still use the exact same Texas Instruments calculator I bought when I was taking some college courses back in, oh, 1990? Maybe 1991. It was for a statistics class. I bought it at the campus bookstore, which used to be right across the street from this wonderful little diner called The Rusty Spoon. They had the most incredible cherry pie. My friend Brenda and I would go there every Tuesday after class. 

Brenda actually moved to Arizona a few years ago because her husband got a job managing a golf course out there. I don't know how she handles the heat, honestly. I completely melt if it gets above eighty degrees here. She sent me a picture of a cactus in her front yard that bloomed last week, and it was pretty, but I just can't imagine living in a desert. She was telling me you have to check your shoes before you put them on because scorpions will hide in them! Can you imagine? Just reaching your foot in and... 

Oh, goodness, I'm so sorry. I completely derailed myself again. Scorpions... what on earth were we talking about? Oh, right, perfection and the checking. Yes. Like I was saying, it has to be perfectly precise. And because I have to do that whole routine over and over until it feels safe, I end up just sitting there at my desk for hours. Some nights it's pitch black outside, everyone else has gone home, and I'm still there with absolutely nothing actually finished.
Do you feel like the things you check need to be perfectly symmetrical or arranged in a very specific way for you to feel calm?

Arranged in a specific way? Yes, definitely. I know I am completely repeating myself here, I'm so sorry, but it really comes down to that set order I mentioned. It’s like a sequence that has to be arranged perfectly. 

Speaking of arranging things, I actually bought this beautiful bamboo desk organizer last weekend to try and keep my workspace a bit more orderly. I found it at that big office supply store on 4th Street. The cashier there, a young man named Leo, was telling me about his golden retriever who just had puppies. Eight puppies! Can you imagine the chaos? He showed me pictures on his phone, and they were just adorable, all piled on top of each other sleeping in this big wicker basket. I love dogs, though my apartment building doesn't allow them. The condo association is incredibly strict about their rules. Just last month they fined Mrs. Gable on the third floor because her welcome mat was supposedly half an inch over the hallway property line. She was furious. She’s lived in that building since 1998, back when the neighborhood was completely different, and she was telling me...

Oh, dear. I completely lost my train of thought again. I am so sorry. You asked about things being arranged a certain way? Right. Well, for me, it's the arrangement of the routine. Like I’ve been saying, to finally calm myself down, I have to go through everything in that exact set order—reopening the spreadsheets, rereading the emails line by line, checking the office locks, and going over the payment confirmations over and over. If I don't do it in that specific sequence, it doesn't feel safe. And that's why I end up stuck at my desk hours later, just exhausted, with absolutely nothing actually finished.
Do you feel like the things you check need to be symmetrical or have a specific pattern for you to feel calm?

A specific pattern? Yes, definitely. I feel like I'm just giving you the exact same answer again, I really do apologize, but yes, that set order I keep mentioning is absolutely a pattern. 

Speaking of patterns, my older sister, Martha, just took up quilting, and she's working on this incredibly complex geometric pattern for her guest bedroom. She bought all the fabric from this lovely little shop downtown that actually used to be an old post office. The woman who runs it, Beatrice, kept all the original brass PO boxes along the back wall, and it is just so charming. Anyway, Martha was telling me that she had to special order this very specific indigo thread because the regular navy blue just washed out completely against the gray squares. She’s always been so particular about colors. Even when we were kids sharing a room, she would organize her crayons by... 

Oh, for heaven's sake, I'm rambling again. I don't know why my brain keeps doing this today, I am so sorry. You asked about patterns and my checking. Right. 

So, like I've been saying, my pattern is that specific sequence. To calm myself down, I just have to do it. I reopen the spreadsheets, I reread the emails line by line, I check the locks, and then I go over the payment confirmations over and over again. It has to be in that exact set order, that pattern, or it just doesn't feel safe to me. And because I get stuck in it, some nights I end up just sitting there at my desk for hours and hours, and I still have absolutely nothing actually finished.
Do you feel like the things you check need to be perfectly arranged or symmetrical for you to feel calm?

Perfectly arranged? Oh, yes. I feel terrible, I really feel like a broken record today, but it all comes back to that same exact sequence. That arrangement of things I have to do. 

You know, talking about arranging things perfectly, I spent about three hours last Sunday just trying to arrange the books on my living room shelves. I have this wonderful collection of old hardcover mysteries—Agatha Christie, mostly, but some Dorothy L. Sayers too. I found this gorgeous first edition of *Murder Must Advertise* at a garage sale last summer. The woman selling it had no idea what it was worth. She was moving to Florida, I think? Or maybe it was Georgia. Somewhere down south because she said she couldn't take another winter here. I don't blame her, honestly, my joints ache so much when it snows. My doctor told me to take turmeric for the inflammation, and I bought a bottle, but the pills are just enormous. I tried cutting one in half, but it crumbled everywhere and stained my kitchen counter yellow for a week! I had to use baking soda and lemon juice to finally get it out, which is a trick my grandmother taught me...

Oh, dear me. I am doing it again. I'm so sorry, I don't know why I can't just stay on topic today. You were asking about things being arranged perfectly? 

Yes, right. Well, like I've been saying, the arrangement that matters to me is the order I check things in. If it's not arranged perfectly, I don't feel calm. So I have to do it all in that set order—reopening the spreadsheets, rereading those emails line by line, checking the locks, and going over the payment confirmations over and over until it finally feels "safe." And because I have to arrange my routine so perfectly, I just get stuck. I'll look up, and it's hours later, the office is completely empty, and I haven't actually finished a single thing.
